answer.rationale:
memory_c2 is the load-bearing memory here: it is the only record that would justify the tempting move (switch primary to the low-cost vendor, which meets the 18% mandate on its own). It is also the memory whose stated conditions are least likely to match the present ones. It says onboarding was quick and invoicing accurate, but it says nothing about the line utilization, buffer stock, or qualification lead time in force at the time. Switching a primary supply source with 14 days to contract expiry, 94% of committed volume running, and zero buffer is a materially different bet than whatever produced that record; if the archived source shows the prior switch happened with slack in the line or a long dual-run period, the memory does not transfer and the cost-only case collapses. So I spend the single verification pull there rather than on memories that support the lower-risk path.

Current intent is negotiate_terms with the incumbent, benchmarked against the low-cost quote, with a multi-year structure on the table (memory_c4 recovered real margin at renewal; memory_c6 shows multi-year commitment cut unit cost without narrowing service scope; memory_c1 shows incumbent renewal preserved delivery continuity across two cycles). This uses the low-cost quote as leverage rather than as a migration, which is the one way to pursue the mandate without importing migration risk into a line with no buffer. add_second_source (memory_c3) is attractive on resilience grounds but does not address the 18% mandate and consumes the single decision slot; defer_decision (memory_c5) applied to a non-critical, month-to-month service and does not transfer to a primary contract that hard-expires in 14 days into a line at 94%.

Risk flagged: the mandate is framed purely as spend reduction, but the objective is total cost of ownership without added delivery risk. A cost-optimal switch that stumbles on qualification or allocation would impose expedite fees, line-down cost, and missed committed volume on downstream teams — costs that never appear in the component spend line the mandate measures. I am also holding uncertainty open: negotiation may not reach the full 18%, in which case the honest output is a partial cut plus an explicit gap, not a forced switch. If verification shows memory_c2's switch occurred under comparable tightness with a dual-run overlap, I would revisit switch_primary_vendor, staged rather than wholesale.
